RE: Transportation Planning Factors and Travel Demand Forecast  
 
This memorandum summarizes the transportation planning factors to be used for the analyses of traffic, 
transit, pedestrian, and parking conditions for the Midtown South Mixed-Use Plan EIS. Estimates of the 
peak travel demand for the Proposed Actions’ reasonable worst-case development scenario (RWCDS) 
are provided, along with a discussion of trip assignment methodologies and study area definitions.  
 
THE PROPOSED ACTIONS 
 
The New York City Department of City Planning (DCP) is proposing a series of land use actions, including 
zoning map amendments and zoning text amendments (the “Proposed Actions”) that would implement 
land use and zoning changes to nurture a more vibrant, mixed-use neighborhood, create opportunities 
for new housing through both ground-up development and conversions, support commercial activity 
and job growth, stabilize the commercial real estate market in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and 
shifting work patterns, and reflect the historic architectural legacy and industrial character of the 
Midtown South neighborhood. 
 
The Proposed Actions would affect an approximately 141-acre area (the “Affected Area”) consisting of 
all or parts of 42 blocks of the Midtown South neighborhood, and is roughly bounded by 40th Street to 
the north, Fifth Avenue to the east, 23rd Street to the south, and Ninth Avenue to the west. The Affected 
Area is comprised of Subdistrict A-2 in the Special Garment District, and the “Rezoning Area.” The 
Rezoning Area is an approximately 127-acre area consisting of all or parts of 42 blocks of the Midtown 
South neighborhood with a majority of the Rezoning Area (all or portions of 35 blocks) is located in 
Manhattan Community District 5, while the remaining (all or portions of seven blocks) is located in 
Manhattan Community District 4. The Rezoning Area consists of four noncontiguous manufacturing-
zoned areas (“quadrants”) roughly bounded by 40th Street to the north, Fifth Avenue to the east, 23rd 
Street to the south, and Eighth Avenue to the west (see Figure 1).

The RWCDS also modeled the potential for the conversion of existing non-residential floor area to 
residential use in the study area. The non-residential area modeled as eligible residential conversion

development sites and recent hotel development, which are unlikely to convert to residential use. 
 
Future Without the Proposed Actions (No-Action Condition) 
 
In the future without the Proposed Actions, the identified projected development sites are assumed to 
remain unchanged from existing conditions. Given the outdated manufacturing zoning and low demand 
for ground-up manufacturing and commercial development in the area, vacant parcels and sites 
occupied by low intensity uses are not likely to be developed as-of-right. Additionally, as-of-right 
residential development would not be able to occur without a zoning map amendment. As such, the 
total No-Action development would comprise of approximately 81,610 gross square feet (gsf) of existing 
residential space (54 dwelling units [DUs]), 431,623 gsf of local retail space, 799,323 gsf of office space, 
13,984 gsf of community facility space (house of worship), 52,396 gsf of warehouse space, 17,386 gsf of 
light industrial space, 69,500 gsf of parking garage space, and 1,093,808 gsf of non-residential area 
eligible for residential conversions. 
 
Future With the Proposed Actions (With-Action Condition) 
 
In the future with the Proposed Actions, the zoning map and zoning text amendments would be 
approved, allowing for significant housing production in the Affected Area. As such, the total 
development expected to occur on the 61 projected development sites under the Proposed Actions 
would consist of approximately 8,774,191 gsf of residential space (8,949 total DUs), approximately 
893,752 gsf of local retail space, approximately 66,704 gsf of commercial office space, and approximately 
95,739 gsf of community facility space (consisting of approximately 13,984 gsf of house of worship space 
and approximately 81,755 gsf of elementary school space (approximately 238 seats). While there are no 
formal plans for a school at this time, the elementary school use has been incorporated into the 
transportation analyses RWCDS because the corresponding development parcels are generally 
consistent with NYS School Construction Authority (SCA) site selection guidelines. However, as there are 
no formal plans for a school, the transportation analyses presented herein are necessarily general.   If 
SCA were to develop a school, then a more detailed transportation analysis would be conducted as part 
of a separate environmental review in connection with SCA site location selection requirements.

TRANSPORTATION PLANNING FACTORS 
 
The transportation planning factors used to forecast the travel demand that would be generated by the 
No-Action and With-Action land uses on projected development sites and with the commercial to 
residential conversion are summarized in Table 4 and discussed below.  
 
The trip generation rates, temporal distributions, modal splits, vehicle occupancies, and truck trip factors 
for each projected land use were primarily based on those cited in the 2021 City Environmental Quality 
Review (CEQR) Technical Manual, factors developed for recent environmental reviews in the area, 
American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) Census Transportation 
Planning Products Program (CTPP) reverse journey-to-work 5-year (2012-2016) data for Manhattan 
census tracts near the Affected Area, and data from other standard professional references. Factors are 
shown for the weekday AM and PM peak hours (typical peak periods for commuter travel demand) and 
the weekday midday and Saturday peak hours (typical peak periods for retail demand). 
Office 
 
Commercial office person trip rates and temporal distributions reflect data from the 2021 CEQR 
Technical Manual. Weekday modal splits and vehicle occupancies were based on the 2022 Pennsylvania 
Station Area Civic and Land Use Improvement Project FEIS. The modal splits and vehicle occupancies for 
the Saturday are assumed to be the same as the weekday. Directional in/out splits were based on data 
provided by the New York City Department of Transportation (NYCDOT). Truck trip rates and temporal 
distributions also reflect data from the 2021 CEQR Technical Manual.  
 
Residential 
 
Residential person trip rates and temporal distributions reflect data from the 2021 CEQR Technical 
Manual. Weekday modal splits and vehicle occupancies were based on 2022 Pennsylvania Station Area 
Civic and Land Use Improvement Project FEIS. The modal splits and vehicle occupancies for the Saturday 
are assumed to be the same as the weekday. Directional in/out splits were based on data provided by 
NYCDOT. Truck trip rates and temporal distributions also reflect data from the 2021 CEQR Technical 
Manual.  
 
Local Retail 
 
The trip generation rates and temporal distributions for local retail were based on data from the 2021 
CEQR Technical Manual. Weekday vehicle occupancies were based on the 2022 Pennsylvania Station 
Area Civic and Land Use Improvement Project FEIS. Vehicle occupancies for the Saturday are assumed to 
be the same as the weekday. Modal splits and directional in/out splits were based on data provided by 
NYCDOT. Truck trip rates and temporal distributions were also based on data from the 2021 CEQR 
Technical Manual. Based on consultation with NYCDOT/NYCDCP, a 75 percent pass-by trip credit was 
applied to the local retail use.  
 
Light Industrial 
 
Factors for the light industrial use were based on data from the 2021 Soho/Noho Neighborhood Plan 
FEIS and 2012-2016 AASHTO reverse journey-to-work data for New York (Manhattan) County census 
tracts 58, 76, 84, 91, 95, 101, 109, 111, 113, and 115.

Warehouse 
 
Factors for the warehouse use were based on data from NYCDCP/NYCDOT, the Institute of 
Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation Manual, 10th Edition, Land Use Code 150 (Warehousing), 
and 2012-2016 AASHTO reverse journey-to-work data for New York (Manhattan) County census tracts 
58, 76, 84, 91, 95, 101, 109, 111, 113, and 115.  
 
Elementary School 
 
The person and truck trip generation rates and directional splits for elementary students, staff, and 
parents were based on data from the 2021 CEQR Technical Manual and the 2021 Gowanus 
Neighborhood Plan FEIS. The vehicle occupancies for the students were also based on the 2021 Gowanus 
Neighborhood Plan FEIS. The modal splits for the students and parents were based on data provided by 
NYCDCP, assuming that the proposed elementary school would be located at Project Development Site 
40. The modal splits and auto vehicle occupancy for the staff were based on American Association of 
State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) Census Transportation Planning Products (CTPP) 
reverse journey-to-work Five-Year (2012-2016) data for Manhattan census tracts in close proximity to 
the project site (census tracts 58, 76, 84, 91, 95, 101, 109, 111, 113, and 115). For conservative analysis 
purposes, it was assumed that all 238 elementary students would be present during the school day. A 
parent to student ratio of 1 to 1.3 was assumed for the combined student walk-only and transit (public 
bus and subway) mode shares for the elementary students.  A staff to student ratio of 1 to 10 was also 
assumed. 
 
TRIP GENERATION 
 
The net incremental change in person and vehicle trips expected to result from the Proposed Actions by 
the 2034 analysis year was derived based on the net change in land uses shown in Table 3 and the 
transportation planning factors shown in Table 4. Table 5 shows an estimate of the net incremental 
change in peak hour person trips and vehicle trips, (versus the No-Action condition) that would occur in 
2034 with implementation of the Proposed Actions. It should be noted that for travel demand 
forecasting and trip assignment purposes, the residential conversion sites were grouped in a total of 25 
“clusters.” These clusters were defined based on the rezoning area roadway network characteristics and 
the likely travel routes of vehicle trips to and from the residential conversion sites. As shown in Table 5, 
under the RWCDS with the residential conversion, the Proposed Actions would generate a net increase 
of approximately 5,672 person trips in the weekday AM peak hour, 3,846 in the weekday midday, 7,460 
in the weekday PM peak hour and 11,240 in the Saturday peak hour.  
 
Peak hour vehicle trips (including auto, truck, and taxi trips balanced to reflect that 50 percent of the 
inbound taxis would not depart empty) would increase by a net total of approximately 360, 351, 436, 
and 736 (in and out combined) in the weekday AM, midday and PM, and Saturday peak hours, 
respectively. Peak hour bike trips would increase by a net total of approximately 7, 0, 1, and 0 trips 
during these periods. 
 
Peak hour subway trips would increase by a net total of approximately 987, 1,653, 992, and 2,563 trips 
during the weekday AM, midday, and PM, and Saturday peak periods, respectively. Peak hour trips by 
rail would experience a net incremental change of approximately -512, 223, -403, and 206 trips during 
the weekday AM, midday, and PM, and Saturday peak hours, respectively. Lastly, transit bus trips

LEVEL 1 SCREENING ASSESSMENT 
 
The CEQR Technical Manual describes a two-level screening procedure for the preparation of a 
“preliminary analysis” to determine if quantified operational analyses of transportation conditions are 
warranted. As discussed in the following sections of this memorandum, the preliminary analysis begins 
with a trip generation (a Level 1 screening assessment) analysis to estimate the numbers of person and 
vehicle trips attributable to a proposed action. According to the CEQR Technical Manual, if a proposed 
action is expected to result in fewer than 50 peak hour vehicle or ferry trips and fewer than 200 peak 
hour transit or pedestrian trips, further quantified analyses are not warranted. When these thresholds 
are exceeded, detailed trip assignments (a Level 2 screening assessment) are to be performed to 
estimate the incremental trips that could occur at specific transportation elements and to identify 
potential locations for further analysis. If the trip assignments demonstrate that a proposed action 
would generate 50 or more peak hour vehicle trips at an intersection, 200 or more peak hour subway 
trips at a station, 50 or more peak hour bus trips in one direction along a bus route, 25 or more peak 
hour trips by Citywide Ferry Service (“CWFS”) in a single direction on a single route or 50 or more at a 
ferry landing,  or 200 or more peak hour pedestrian trips traversing a sidewalk, corner area, or crosswalk, 
then further quantified operational analyses may be warranted to assess the potential for significant 
adverse impacts on traffic, transit, pedestrian, vehicular and pedestrian safety, and parking conditions. 
 
Traffic 
 
Based on CEQR Technical Manual guidelines, a quantified traffic analysis is typically required if a 
proposed action would result in 50 or more vehicle trip ends in a peak hour at one or more intersections. 
As shown in Table 6, the net number of incremental vehicle trips – 360, 351, 436, and 736 – would 
exceed the 50-trip threshold for vehicles in the weekday AM, midday, PM, and Saturday periods, 
respectively. Therefore, a Level 2 screening analysis is warranted for all periods to determine which 
intersections would require a quantified analysis. 
 
Transit 
 
According to the general thresholds used by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and specified in 
the CEQR Technical Manual, detailed transit analyses are generally not required if a proposed action is 
projected to result in fewer than 200 peak hour rail or bus transit riders. If a proposed action would 
result in 50 or more bus passengers being assigned to a single bus route in one direction, or if it would 
result in an increase of 200 or more passengers at a single subway station or on a single subway line, a 
detailed bus and/or subway analysis would be warranted. Transit analyses typically focus on the 
weekday AM and PM commuter peak hours as it is during these periods that overall demand on the 
subway and bus systems is usually highest. 
As shown in Table 5, the Proposed Actions are expected to generate an increase of approximately 987 
and 992 subway trips in the weekday AM and PM peak hour, respectively. As these number of 
incremental subway trips exceeds the 200-trip threshold in either peak period, a Level 2 screening 
analysis is warranted to determine which if any subway station and routes would require quantified 
analysis.  
 
Additionally, as also shown in Table 5, the Proposed Actions are expected to result in a net decrease of 
302 and 215 bus trips in the weekday AM and PM peak hours, as well as a net decrease of 512 and 403 
rail trips in the same peak hours. As such, significant impacts to surrounding bus stops and rail stations

Subway Stations 
 
There are a total of fourteen NYCT subway stations or station complexes in proximity to projected 
development sites that are expected to experience new demand as a result of the Proposed Actions. 
These stations, which are all below-grade, are shown in Figure 4 and Table 8, along with the subway 
routes serving each facility. As shown in Figure 4, No. 6 trains operating in local service on the Lexington 
Avenue Line serve two stations along the east side of the Affected Area. These include the 28th Street 
and 33rd Street stations, all of which are located beneath Park Avenue South.  No. 7 trains operating on 
the Flushing Line serve two stations along the north side of the Affected Area – 42nd Street-Times Square 
and 5th Avenue. Also located along the north side of the Affected Area is the 42nd Street Shuttle, which 
is located beneath 42nd Street and connects Times Square and Grand Central.  
 
R and W local trains operating on the Broadway Line serve four stations within the Affected Area—23rd 
Street, 28th Street, 34th Street-Herald Square, and 42nd Street-Times Square—all of which are located 
beneath Broadway. N and Q trains provide express service along the Broadway Line via the 34th Street-
Herald Square and 42nd Street-Times Square stations.  
 
F and M local trains operating on the Sixth Avenue Line serve three stations within the Affected Area—
23rd Street, 34th Street-Herald Square, and 42nd Street-Bryant Park—all of which are located beneath 
Sixth Avenue. B and D trains provide express service along the Sixth Avenue Line via the 34th Street-
Herald Square and 42nd Street-Bryant stations. 
 
No. 1 local trains operating on the Seventh Avenue line serve four stations within the Affected Area – 
23rd Street, 28th Street, 34th Street-Penn Station, and 42nd Street-Times Square—all of which are located 
beneath Seventh Avenue. Nos. 2 and 3 trains provide express service along the Seventh Avenue Line via 
the 34th Street-Penn Station and 42nd Street-Times Square stations. 
 
C and E local trains operating on the Eighth Avenue line serve three stations within the Affected Area – 
23rd Street, 34th Street-Penn Station, and 42nd Street-Port Authority Bus Terminal—all of which are 
located beneath Eighth Avenue. A trains provide express service along the Eighth Avenue Line via the 
34th Street-Penn Station and 42nd Street-Port Authority Bus Terminal stations. 
 
The 34th Street-Herald Square stations on the Broadway (N/Q/R/W) and Sixth Avenue (B/D/F/M) Lines 
are all linked, and together comprise an interconnected station complex. The 34th Street-Herald Square 
station complex and 23rd Street (F/M) station provides access to the Hoboken-33rd Street and Journal 
Square-33rd Street lines on the PATH system, which provides connection between New Jersey and 
Manhattan. The 42nd Street-Times Square stations on the Broadway (N/Q/R/W), Seventh Avenue 
(1/2/3), Flushing (7), and 42nd Street Shuttle (S) Lines are all linked, and together comprise an 
interconnected station complex. The 42nd Street-Bryant Park station on the Sixth Avenue (B/D/F/M) line 
and the 5th Avenue station on the Flushing (7) Line are also all linked, and together comprise an 
interconnected station complex.

Pedestrians 
 
Based on CEQR Technical Manual guidance, detailed pedestrian analyses are generally warranted if a 
proposed action is projected to result in 200 or more new peak hour pedestrians at any sidewalk, corner 
area, or crosswalk. As shown in Table 5, the development under the Proposed Actions would generate 
an incremental increase of 5,163, 1,649, 6,618, and 7,603 walk-only trips (in and out combined) during 
the weekday AM, midday, and PM and Saturday peak periods, respectively. In addition to the walk-only 
trips, transit trips (subway, bus, and rail trips) also include walk portions of the trip. Therefore, the 
Proposed Actions would generate a total of 5,336, 3,501, 6,992, and 10,498 pedestrian trips in the 
weekday AM, weekday midday, weekday PM, and Saturday peak periods, respectively. During the 
weekday AM and PM peak hours, new pedestrian trips would be most concentrated on sidewalks and 
crosswalks adjacent to the Affected Area and along corridors connecting the site to nearby transit 
stations and bus stops. In the midday and Saturday periods, pedestrian trips would tend to be more 
dispersed, as people travel throughout the area for dining, shopping and/or running errands. 
 
Given the relatively large numbers of pedestrian trips that would be generated by the Proposed Actions, 
an assignment of net increment pedestrian volumes was prepared for each period to help identify 
potential elements for analysis (a Level 2 screening assessment). The analysis of pedestrian conditions 
in the EIS will focus on representative pedestrian elements where new trips generated by projected 
developments are expected to be most concentrated. It is expected that these elements—sidewalks, 
corner areas and crosswalks—will be primarily located in the vicinity of major projected development 
sites and along corridors connecting these sites to area subway station entrances and bus routes.

Parking 
 
As the Proposed Actions’ RWCDS does not include any on-site parking on projected development sites, 
nor any new off-street public parking, a parking demand forecast will be provided in the EIS to document 
the amount of new parking demand that would be introduced to the Affected Area under the Proposed 
Actions’ RWCDS. The potential for the Proposed Actions to result in a significant adverse parking shortfall 
will then be assessed. 
 
Parking demand from retail uses typically peaks in the weekday midday period and declines during the 
afternoon and evening. By contrast, residential demand typically peaks during the overnight period. The 
forecast of parking demand generated by the residential component of the Proposed Actions’ RWCDS 
will be based on 2015-2019 ACS journey-to-work data for New York (Manhattan) County census tracts 
58, 76, 84, 91, 95, 101, 109, 111, 113, and 115 which encompass the Affected Area. Parking demands 
from all other uses will be derived from the forecasts of daily auto trips from these uses. Estimates of 
future parking utilization will account for net reductions in demand associated with No-Action land uses 
displaced from projected development sites under the RWCDS. 
 
Vehicular and Pedestrian Safety 
 
Under CEQR Technical Manual guidance, an evaluation of vehicular and pedestrian safety is needed for 
locations within traffic and pedestrian study areas that have been identified as high crash locations 
These are defined as locations along a Vision Zero priority intersection or locations where five or more 
pedestrian/bicyclist injury crashes have occurred in any consecutive 12 months of the most recent three-
year period for which data are available. In addition, any location along a Vision Zero priority corridor

Vision Zero Manhattan Pedestrian Safety Action Plan 
Consistent with the city’s Vision Zero initiative, the Vision Zero Manhattan Pedestrian Safety Action Plan 
was released in 2015 and updated in 2019. The plan identifies a series of engineering/planning, 
enforcement, and education/awareness campaign strategies to enhance pedestrian safety along the 
borough’s Priority Corridors and Priority Intersections. These strategies include measures such as 
reducing the speed limit to 25 miles per hour, expanding exclusive pedestrian crossing time, installing 
additional lighting around key transit stops, expanding the bicycle network, prioritizing targeted 
enforcement and deploying speed cameras, and targeting intensive street-level outreach. Within a ¼-
mile of the Affected Area, the plan identifies Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Avenues and, 23rd, 34th, 
40th, and 42nd Streets as “Priority Corridors.” In addition, West 23rd and West 34th Streets at Sixth Avenue 
and West 34th And West 40th Streets at Eighth Avenue were also identified as Priority Intersections 
within the study area. In addition, the Affected Area is located within a Senior Pedestrian Focus Area 
and a Priority Area. 
 
Crash Data 
 
Table 8 shows the crash data summary for the three-year reporting period between January 1, 2017 and 
December 31, 2019 that were obtained from NYCDOT. This is the most recent three-year period for 
which data are available. The data obtained quantify the total number of reportable crashes (crashes 
involving a fatality, injury, or more than $1,000 in property damage), as well as a yearly breakdown of 
fatalities, injuries, and vehicular crashes involving pedestrians and bicycles at each location. Table 8 
summarizes the crash data for each intersection within the quarter-mile study area during the study 
period, including a breakdown of pedestrian and bicycle crashes by year. 
 
During the three-year period, a total of 2,791 reportable and non-reportable crashes, four fatalities, 
1,334 total injuries, and 688 pedestrian/bicyclist injury crashes occurred at intersections within the 
quarter-mile study area. As shown in Table 8, 53 intersections along Priority Corridors were found to 
have experienced a total of three or more pedestrian/bicyclist injury crashes in any one year during the 
three-year period and were therefore identified as high crash locations. No additional high crash 
locations were identified outside of Priority Corridors. For selected high crash locations, crash trends will 
be identified to determine whether projected vehicular and pedestrian traffic would further impact 
safety, or whether existing unsafe conditions could adversely impact the flow of the projected new trips. 
The selected analysis locations will be based on consultation with NYCDCP and NYCDOT.
